title: MANAGING FILES FROM THE COMMAND LINE
display: Ch 3 — MANAGING FILES FROM THE COMMAND LINE

content.text: Book reference: Chapter 3, pages 47–100. Guided Exercises: Managing Files Using Command-line Tools, Making Links Between Files. Lab: Managing Files from the Command Line.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter
File and directory manipulation is core, hands-on RHCSA material — expect to create, copy, move, delete, and link files under time pressure. Everything below is fair game.

Every file on a RHEL system lives in one single inverted tree rooted at / (there's no separate "C: drive" concept — even a second disk just gets attached, or "mounted", onto a directory somewhere under /). Standardized subdirectories keep files organized by purpose:
| Directory | Purpose |
| /usr | Installed software, libraries, read-only program data. /usr/bin (user commands), /usr/sbin (admin commands), /usr/local (locally added software). |
| /etc | Configuration files for this system. |
| /var | Variable data that should survive a reboot — logs, databases, spool files, website content. |
| /run | Runtime data for currently-running processes (PID files, locks) — wiped and recreated every boot. |
| /home | Regular users' personal files and settings. |
| /root | Home directory for the root superuser (not the same as /). |
| /tmp | World-writable scratch space; files untouched for 10 days are auto-deleted (/var/tmp uses 30 days). |
| /boot | Files needed to start the boot process. |
| /dev | Special device files representing hardware. |
NOTE — Legacy /bin, /sbin, /lib
In RHEL 7 and later, /bin, /sbin, /lib, and /lib64 are symbolic links into their /usr equivalents — a legacy split that no longer reflects separate content, kept only for compatibility.

sections.title: 3.2 Absolute vs. relative paths, and moving around

content.text: | Path type | Rule | Example |
| Absolute | Starts with / — a complete address from the root. | /var/log/messages |
| Relative | Doesn't start with / — read from wherever you currently are. | log/messages (if you're already in /var) |
WARNING — Case sensitivity
Linux filesystems (ext4, XFS, etc.) are case-sensitive — File.txt and file.txt are two different files. This trips people up coming from Windows/macOS, where the filesystem often isn't.
| Command | Effect |
| pwd | Print full path of the current ("working") directory. |
| ls | List directory contents. -l long format, -a include hidden (dotfile) entries, -R recurse into subdirectories. |
| cd <path> | Change directory. cd alone (no argument) goes home. |
| cd - | Jump back to whatever directory you were in immediately before this one — great for bouncing between two locations. |
| cd .. | Move up one level to the parent directory. |
| cd . | Stay put — "." always means "here", useful as a destination argument, e.g. cp somefile . |
| touch <file> | Update a file's timestamp, creating it empty if it doesn't exist yet — the standard way to make a quick test file. |
Hidden files (names starting with a dot, like .bashrc) don't show in a plain ls — this exists to keep config clutter out of your way, not as a security measure. Use ls -a to see them.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Command reference
This table is the single most exam-relevant table in this chapter — know every row cold.
| Task | Command |
| Create a directory | `mkdir directory` |
| Create parent dirs too if missing | `mkdir -p a/b/c` |
| Copy a file | `cp file new-file` |
| Copy a directory + contents | `cp -r directory new-directory` |
| Move or rename | `mv file new-file` |
| Remove a file | `rm file` |
| Remove a directory + contents | `rm -r directory` |
| Remove an empty directory | `rmdir directory` (or `rm -d`) |
WARNING — cp and mv overwrite silently

If the destination file already exists, cp and mv replace it with no confirmation and no way to undo it — there's no command-line trash bin. Double-check destinations before you run these, especially with wildcards.

mkdir -p is convenient but dangerous if you mistype a path — it will happily create the misspelled directory instead of erroring, silently putting your files in the wrong place. A plain mkdir without -p at least fails loudly ("No such file or directory") when a parent is missing, which is often the safer default while you're still typing carefully.

rm -r deletes recursively without asking. Add -i to be prompted per file/directory (rm -ri), or -f to force through without any prompts at all — and note -f always wins if you accidentally combine -i and -f.
cp on its own ignores directories entirely ("cp: omitting directory") unless you add -r — a common source of "why didn't my folder copy" confusion.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Links
Creating and distinguishing hard vs. soft links is a standard RHCSA task — know both ln syntaxes and how to tell them apart with ls -l.
Every file starts life as a single hard link — a name pointing at the actual data on disk. ln creates another name pointing at that same data:
ln existing-file new-hardlink-name

Both names are now completely equivalent — same content, same permissions/ownership, same timestamps, because they point at identical data. ls -l shows a link count (the small number just after the permissions) — 2 once a second hard link exists. Data is only actually erased once the last hard link to it is removed, so deleting the "original" name is harmless as long as another hard link survives.
| Limitation of hard links | Why |
| Can't link a directory | Not allowed by the filesystem, to prevent loops in the directory tree. |

| Can't cross filesystems | A hard link is just another name inside the same on-disk data structure — it can't reach across to a different mounted filesystem. Check with df which "Mounted on" boundary two paths fall under. |
Soft (symbolic) links avoid both limits — they're a small special file that just stores a path to another file or directory:
ln -s /path/to/target /path/to/link-name
ls -l shows soft links starting with l (versus - for a regular file or d for a directory), with -> target after the name.
💡 Why this matters — The core mental model
A hard link points a name directly at data on disk. A soft link points a name at another name, which then points at the data.

Consequence: delete the file a soft link points to, and the link goes "dangling" (points at nothing, cat fails with "No such file or directory") — but the link itself still exists. If you later create a new file at that same path, the dangling link starts working again automatically, pointing at whatever's there now. Hard links can't do this: once the target is truly gone, an old hard link name is disconnected from any future file created with that same name.

sections.title: 3.5 Shell expansions — pattern matching, brace expansion, quoting

content.text: RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Globbing
Wildcards are how you operate on many files in one command — a routine efficiency expectation on the exam, not just a convenience.
| Pattern | Matches |
| `*` | Any string of zero or more characters |
| `?` | Exactly one character |
| `[abc]` | One character, any of a, b, or c |
| `[!abc]` or `[^abc]` | One character, anything except a, b, or c |
| `[[:alpha:]]` | One alphabetic character |
| `[[:digit:]]` | One digit 0–9 |
| `[[:upper:]]` / `[[:lower:]]` | One uppercase / lowercase letter |
Given files able alfa baker bravo cast charlie delta dog easy echo:
ls a* → able alfa
ls *a* → able alfa baker bravo cast charlie delta easy
ls [ac]* → able alfa cast charlie
ls ???? → able alfa cast easy echo (any 4-character name)
Tilde expansion
~ expands to your home directory; ~username expands to that user's home directory. echo ~ is a quick way to check what it resolves to.
Brace expansion
Braces generate every combination of a comma list or a range, which is the fastest way to create (or reference) many related names in one command:
echo file{1..3}.txt → file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt
echo file{a,b}{1,2}.txt → filea1.txt filea2.txt fileb1.txt fileb2.txt
mkdir project/{src,docs,tests} # three directories, one command
Variable and command substitution
NAME=operator; echo $NAME # → operator
echo Today is $(date +%A). # command substitution: runs date, drops its output in
Quoting — controlling what does and doesn't expand
| Quoting | Effect |
| `\` (backslash) | Escapes just the next single character — e.g. `\$HOME` prints literally $HOME instead of expanding it. |
| "double quotes" | Blocks globbing/wildcards, but still allows $variable and $(command) substitution. |
| 'single quotes' | Blocks everything — the most literal option. |
WARNING — Don't confuse ' with `

The single quote (') and the backtick (`, the old-style command-substitution character) look and sit similarly on the keyboard but behave completely differently. Prefer $(command) over backticks — it's clearer and, unlike backticks, nests cleanly.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: A condensed version of the book's two Guided Exercises and Lab, adapted to run directly on servera (no lab scripts needed):
1. ssh student@servera, then mkdir Music Pictures Videos.
2. touch song{1..6}.mp3 snap{1..6}.jpg film{1..6}.avi — twelve files, one command each set.
3. mv song*.mp3 Music/ ; mv snap*.jpg Pictures/ ; mv film*.avi Videos/ — sort them by type.
4. mkdir friends family work, then cp Music/song1.mp3 Pictures/snap1.jpg friends/ (mix file types into one destination).
5. rmdir friends — watch it fail ("Directory not empty"), then rm -r friends to actually clear it out.
6. touch source.file; ln source.file source.hardlink; ls -l source.* — confirm both show link count 2.
7. ln -s /tmp tempdir; ls -l tempdir — confirm the l at the start of the permissions and the -> /tmp target.
8. rm source.file; cat source.hardlink still works (data survives); but if you'd soft-linked instead, cat would now fail — try it to see the difference for yourself.
1. Q1 — You run rm -r project and immediately regret it. What actually happens next, and what does that imply about double-checking commands before running them?
2. Q2 — Two files show the same inode number under ls -i. What does that tell you, and what's one thing that could prevent you from creating that relationship between two particular paths?
3. Q3 — Write a single wildcard pattern that matches only filenames that are at least three characters long.
NOTE — Answers

Q1 — There is no undo and no trash bin on the command line; the directory and its contents are gone immediately. This is exactly why it's worth running pwd and ls before any rm -r, especially with wildcards.

Q2 — Identical inode numbers mean the two names are hard links to the same underlying data. You can't create that relationship across two different mounted filesystems (check with df which mount boundary each path falls under), and you can't hard-link a directory at all.
Q3 — ???* (three characters of any kind, followed by * for zero or more additional characters).
- Linux files live in one inverted tree from /; /etc, /var, /home, /tmp, /usr are the directories to know by purpose.
- Absolute paths start with /; relative paths are read from the current working directory. cd -, cd .., and cd . are the fast-navigation shortcuts.
- mkdir, cp, mv, rm(-r), rmdir are the core file-management toolkit — cp/mv overwrite silently, rm has no undo.
- Hard links share the same underlying data (same inode, can't cross filesystems, can't target a directory); soft links are a separate file that stores a path, and can dangle.
- Glob patterns (*, ?, [abc], [[:digit:]]...), brace expansion ({1..3}), and quoting (", ', \) let you operate on many files precisely and efficiently.
